title: Percentage
summary: The language of the whole arithmetic section — profit-loss, interest, discount and DI are all percentage questions in disguise. Tier 1 asks 1–2 direct questions per shift (successive change, more/less flips, election and population problems) and Tier 2 leans on it heavily.

subtopics.title: Percentage meaning & conversions
subtopics.concept:
Per cent means per hundred: $x\% = \frac{x}{100}$. The single most profitable memorisation in Quant is the fraction table — every CGL percentage, profit-loss, interest and DI question gets faster.

| Fraction | % | Fraction | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | 50% | $\frac{1}{8}$ | 12.5% |
| $\frac{1}{3}$ | $33\frac{1}{3}\%$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ | 37.5% |
| $\frac{2}{3}$ | $66\frac{2}{3}\%$ | $\frac{5}{8}$ | 62.5% |
| $\frac{1}{4}$ | 25% | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $16\frac{2}{3}\%$ |
| $\frac{3}{4}$ | 75% | $\frac{5}{6}$ | $83\frac{1}{3}\%$ |
| $\frac{1}{5}$ | 20% | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $14\frac{2}{7}\%$ |
| $\frac{2}{5}$ | 40% | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $11\frac{1}{9}\%$ |
| $\frac{1}{12}$ | $8\frac{1}{3}\%$ | $\frac{1}{16}$ | 6.25% |

**Handy symmetry:** $x\%$ of $y = y\%$ of $x$ (16% of 25 = 25% of 16).

$p\%$ of a quantity $N = \frac{pN}{100}$; to find the whole when a part is known, divide: $N = \frac{\text{part} \times 100}{p}$.

formulas.name: Commutativity
formulas.tex: x\% \text{ of } y = y\% \text{ of } x

tricks.title: The fraction table IS the shortcut
tricks.body: Convert percentages to fractions before multiplying: 12.5% of 640 = 1/8 × 640 = 80. One line, no calculator.

tricks.title: Swap the percentages
tricks.body: Use $x\%$ of $y = y\%$ of $x$ when the swapped pair is friendlier.

tricks.title: Part-to-whole in one division
tricks.body: 'p% of a number is k' ⇒ number = 100k/p. Look at options: only one will make the product land on k.

example.q: If 40% of a number is 256, find the number.

mistakes: Treating $x\%$ of $y$ as $xy$ (missing the ÷100).
Converting 1/8 as 18% instead of 12.5%.
Dividing by the wrong base: % change must always use the ORIGINAL value as denominator.
Reading 'B's income is x% of A's' as 'x% more than A's'.

subtopics.title: Percentage increase / decrease & successive change
subtopics.concept:
Percentage change $= \frac{\text{final} - \text{initial}}{\text{initial}} \times 100$ (initial = the base being changed).

**Two successive changes** of $a\%$ and $b\%$ combine to $a + b + \frac{ab}{100}$ (keep minus signs for decreases).

+10% then −10% is **not** zero: net $= -\frac{10^2}{100} = -1\%$ (a fall of a²/100 %).

To restore an original value after a multiplier, divide back: if $F = I \times \frac{120}{100}$ then $I = F \times \frac{100}{120}$.

Model every change as a fraction multiplier: +20% → ×6/5, −25% → ×3/4. Chain the multipliers.

formulas.name: Successive change
formulas.note: use signs: + for increase, − for decrease

tricks.title: Multiplier chaining
tricks.body: Replace every % by its fraction multiplier and multiply across all steps.

example.q: A number is increased by 20% and the result is decreased by 10%. Net change?

tricks.title: a + b + ab/100 in one line
tricks.body: Add, then adjust by the product term. Fastest when one change is small.

tricks.title: Reverse to the original
tricks.body: To undo +25%, divide by 5/4 (not multiply by 75/100).

example.q: After a 25% increase a salary is ₹50,000. What was it before?

mistakes: Adding successive percentages without the $\frac{ab}{100}$ term.
Assuming +x% followed by −x% is a net zero.
Using the new (increased) value as the base when computing a percentage decrease.
Undoing +25% by applying −25% (the right move is ÷1.25).

subtopics.title: 'x% more than' ↔ 'x% less than' & chains
subtopics.concept:
The 'more than / less than' pair has **different bases** — this asymmetry is tested constantly.

- If A is $x\%$ **more** than B: $A = B\left(1 + \frac{x}{100}\right)$, and B is $\frac{100x}{100 + x}\%$ **less** than A.
- If A is $x\%$ **less** than B: $A = B\left(1 - \frac{x}{100}\right)$, and B is $\frac{100x}{100 - x}\%$ **more** than A.

**Chains:** if A = a% of B and B = b% of C, then A $= \frac{ab}{100}\%$ of C.

The 'less than' percentage is always LARGER than the 'more than' percentage — use that to sanity-check options.

formulas.name: Less → more
formulas.tex: A = B\left(1 - \frac{x}{100}\right) \Rightarrow \text{B is } \frac{100x}{100-x}\% \text{ more than A}

tricks.title: Flip with 100x/(100±x)
tricks.body: More→less uses 100+x in the denominator; less→more uses 100−x. The answer must be bigger than x for the less→more direction.

example.q: A's salary is 25% more than B's. B's salary is what per cent less than A's?

tricks.title: Assume the base = 100
tricks.body: Set the unmentioned quantity to 100 and read off both values.

example.q: A's salary is 20% more than B's. By what per cent is B's salary less than A's?

tricks.title: Chain percentages by multiplying fractions
tricks.body: Convert each link to a fraction of the next and multiply.

example.q: A's income is 40% of B's, and B's is 25% of C's. A's income is what % of C's?

mistakes: Answering 'x% less' with the same x (the correct value $\frac{100x}{100+x}$ is always smaller than x).
Using 100 − x in the denominator for the more→less direction.
Chaining by adding percentages instead of multiplying fractions.
Ignoring which quantity the question calls the base.

subtopics.title: Population growth, depreciation & elections
subtopics.concept:
**Population / value growth-decay:** value after n years $= P\left(1 \pm \frac{r}{100}\right)^n$ (+ for growth, − for depreciation). Work backwards by dividing.

**Two different rates** in two years: apply the multipliers one after another (e.g. ×11/10 then ×19/20).

**Election problems:** total votes polled = valid + invalid. Both candidates' shares must be read off the VALID votes. Margin = difference of shares × valid votes.

Depreciation is the same formula with a negative rate: present $= P\left(\frac{100-r}{100}\right)^n$.

tricks.title: Multiplier chips for n years
tricks.body: Chips: +10% → 11/10, −5% → 19/20. Multiply chips across years; the final fraction tells everything.

example.q: A town's population of 40,000 grows 10% in year 1 and falls 5% in year 2. Find the present population.

tricks.title: Work backwards with division
tricks.body: For 'value n years ago', divide by the chips instead of guessing.

example.q: A machine worth ₹8,100 depreciates at 10% p.a. What was its value 2 years ago?
example.solution: Divide by the chip twice: ₹$8100 \times \frac{10}{9} = 9000$, then $9000 \times \frac{10}{9} = 10000$.

tricks.title: Elections: everything on valid votes
tricks.body: Convert both candidates' data to fractions of valid votes; the total polled number then follows from the margin.

example.q: In an election, 20% of votes polled were invalid. The winner got 60% of valid votes and won by 1200 votes. Total votes polled?
example.solution: Margin = 20% of valid = $\frac{1}{5}V = 1200$ ⇒ V = 6000 = 80% of total ⇒ total = 7500.

mistakes: Applying $\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^n$ when the two years have different rates.
Counting invalid votes as a candidate's votes.
Depreciating 2 years as $P - 2r\%$ instead of $\left(\frac{90}{100}\right)^2$.
In 'population 2 years ago' questions, dividing by (1 + net%) with the averaged rate.

subtopics.title: Marks, income–expenditure–savings & price–consumption
subtopics.concept:
**Pass-marks template:** candidate 1 scores $p\%$ and fails by $f$ marks ⇒ pass mark $= \frac{pM}{100} + f$; candidate 2 scores $q\%$ and exceeds by $e$ ⇒ pass mark $= \frac{qM}{100} - e$. Equate and solve for maximum marks $M$.

**Income–expenditure:** savings = income − expenditure. If income is I and savings s%, expenditure = (100 − s)% of I.

**Price rises, keep expenditure fixed:** consumption must fall by $\frac{100r}{100 + r}\%$.
**Price falls, same quantity-money:** extra quantity bought $= \frac{\text{money} \times r}{100 \times \text{reduced price}}$; reduced price $= \frac{r\% \text{ of outlay}}{\text{extra quantity}}$.

formulas.name: Price cut & extra quantity
formulas.tex: \text{reduced price} = \frac{r\% \text{ of outlay}}{\text{extra quantity}},\quad \text{old price} = \frac{\text{reduced price}}{1 - r/100}

tricks.title: Marks gap = percentage gap
tricks.body: In two-candidate mark problems the difference of the two percentages times M equals the total mark gap (fail-by + exceed-by).

example.q: A candidate scoring 33% fails by 45 marks; another scoring 45% gets 15 marks more than the pass mark. Find the maximum marks.

tricks.title: Income = 100 bookkeeping
tricks.body: Set income to 100, express savings and expenditure, then apply every change and read the answer off.

example.q: A man saves 20% of his income. His income rises 15% and expenditure rises 10%. % increase in savings?
example.solution: Income 100 → save 20, spend 80. New: income 115, spend 88 ⇒ save 27. Increase = 7/20 = 35%.

tricks.title: Price cut: r% of money buys the extra
tricks.body: A r% price cut saves r% of the outlay, and that saved money buys the extra quantity at the REDUCED price.

example.q: A 20% cut in sugar price lets a buyer get 5 kg more for ₹400. Find the original price.
example.solution: Saved money = 20% of 400 = ₹80 = price of extra 5 kg ⇒ reduced price ₹16/kg ⇒ original price = ₹$16 \times \frac{100}{80}$ = ₹20 per kg.

mistakes: Using the fail-by and exceed-by marks with the same sign (they act in opposite directions: +f and −e on the two sides).
In savings problems, raising expenditure by 10% as 'reduce savings by 10%'.
For the price-cut question, dividing the full outlay (not r% of it) by the extra quantity.
Consumption reduction for a 25% price rise answered as 25% instead of 20%.

pyqPatterns.pattern: x% of a number / fraction conversion
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'What is 35% of 480', '1/8 as a percentage', 'if p% of N is k find N'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fraction table + one multiplication or division. Under 30 seconds; never long-multiply.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two or three changes applied one after another (price/population/marks), asking net change or final value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Multiplier chips (×6/5, ×3/4 …) or a + b + ab/100. For up-then-down by the same rate, remember the −x²/100 rule.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'A's income is 25% more than B's; B's income is what % less than A's?'
pyqPatterns.approach: $\frac{100x}{100+x}$ (more→less) or $\frac{100x}{100-x}$ (less→more). Assume the base = 100 to verify.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Population grows/falls at stated yearly rates (same or different); find present, past, or future value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Chain the multipliers forward; divide by them to go back. Two different rates: never average them, multiply chips.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two candidates, invalid votes given, winner's share of valid votes and margin given; find total votes or votes got.
pyqPatterns.approach: Work everything in fractions of VALID votes; margin% × valid votes = margin; then unmask the total.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One candidate fails by f marks at p%, another exceeds pass by e at q%; find maximum marks or pass mark.
pyqPatterns.approach: % gap × M = f + e. Solve M, then pass mark from either candidate.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Price rises 20%, by what % reduce consumption to keep expenditure same' or the reverse (5 kg more for a fixed outlay).
pyqPatterns.approach: Consumption factor = new expenditure factor ÷ price factor. For the outlay version, r% of money = extra quantity × reduced price.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Savings % given; income and expenditure change by given %; find % change in savings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Set income = 100, track all three quantities with chips, compute the new savings directly.

solvedExamples.q: A number is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net percentage change?
Find the value of $16\frac{2}{3}\%$ of 720 $+$ $33\frac{1}{3}\%$ of 450.
The price of an article is first increased by 10% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net change in price?
solvedExamples.solution:
Net $= 10 - 10 - \frac{10 \times 10}{100} = -1\%$.
A rise of 10% followed by a fall of 10% always leaves a **1% decrease**.

solvedExamples.q: A's salary is 25% more than B's salary. B's salary is what per cent less than A's salary?
The value of a machine depreciates at the rate of 10% per annum. If its present value is ₹8,100, what was its value 2 years ago?
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the value 2 years ago be P.
$P\left(\frac{90}{100}\right)^2 = 8100$
$P \times \frac{81}{100} = 8100$, so P = ₹10,000.

practice.q: If 40% of a number is 256, then 55% of that number is:
Expressed as a percentage, $\frac{3}{8}$ is equal to:
The price of an article falls from ₹250 to ₹200. The percentage decrease in price is:
In a class of 60 students, 65% are boys. The number of girls in the class is:
practice.shortcut: 35% of 60 = 21. (39 is the number of boys — the trap.)

practice.q: In an election between two candidates, 20% of the votes polled were invalid. The winner secured 60% of the valid votes and won by a margin of 1,200 votes. How many votes were polled in total?
practice.solution:
Let total polled = T; valid = 0.8T.
Winner gets 60% of valid, loser 40%; margin = 20% of valid.
$0.2 \times 0.8T = 1200$ ⇒ $0.16T = 1200$ ⇒ T = 7500.
practice.shortcut: Margin is 1/5 of valid votes ⇒ valid = 6000 = 80% of total ⇒ total 7500.

practice.q: The population of a town two years ago was 40,000. It increased by 10% in the first year and decreased by 5% in the second year. The present population is:
practice.shortcut: Chips 11/10 × 19/20. Never average the rates (net is +4.5%, not +5%).

practice.q: In an examination, a candidate scoring 33% marks fails by 45 marks, while another candidate scoring 45% marks gets 15 marks more than the pass marks. What are the maximum marks?
A's income is 20% more than B's income. B's income is less than A's income by:
practice.solution:
Let B = 100, then A = 120.
B is short of A by 20 on base 120 ⇒ $\frac{20}{120} \times 100 = 16\frac{2}{3}\%$.

practice.q: The price of rice increases by 20%. By what per cent must a family reduce its consumption so that the expenditure on rice increases by only 8%?
practice.solution:
Consumption factor $= \frac{\text{expenditure factor}}{\text{price factor}} = \frac{108}{120} = \frac{9}{10}$.
So consumption must be cut by **10%**.
practice.shortcut: 1.08 ÷ 1.20 = 0.90 ⇒ reduce 10%. (20% is the trap from the standard 'same expenditure' rule.)

practice.q: If the numerator of a fraction is increased by 20% and the denominator is decreased by 10%, the fraction becomes:
A man spends 80% of his income. His income increases by 15% and his expenditure increases by 10%. The percentage increase in his savings is:
practice.solution:
Take income = 100 ⇒ expenditure = 80, savings = 20.
New income = 115, new expenditure = 88 ⇒ new savings = 27.
Increase $= \frac{7}{20} \times 100 = 35\%$.
practice.shortcut: Track the three quantities on income = 100. Savings go 20 → 27 = +35%.

practice.q: A's salary is 40% of B's salary and B's salary is 25% of C's salary. A's salary is what per cent of C's salary?
The population of a village increased by 20% in the first year, by 25% in the second year and by 10% in the third year. If the present population is 66,000, what was it 3 years ago?
A reduction of 20% in the price of sugar enables a person to buy 5 kg more sugar for ₹400. The original price of sugar per kg is:
practice.solution:
Money saved due to the cut = 20% of ₹400 = ₹80.
This ₹80 buys the extra 5 kg at the reduced price ⇒ reduced price = ₹16/kg.
Original price = ₹$16 \times \frac{100}{80}$ = ₹20 per kg.
practice.shortcut: r% of outlay ÷ extra kg = reduced price (80/5 = 16); original = reduced ÷ 0.8 = 20.
